web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: Why the Stock Trades Here — Market Expectations vs. Peers
question: What growth, margin, and cash-conversion miracle is already baked into ₹2,455.90 (116x TTM earnings), and how does AZAD compare head-to-head against listed Indian aerospace and precision-forging peers?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a stock prices in ten years of flawless compounding before the first rupee of free cash flow arrives, the margin of safety is zero.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk

web_blocks.title: Deconstructing ₹2,455.90: Multiple Expansion vs. Capital Intensity

web_blocks.html: As of the verified 2026-11-13 NSE close, Azad Engineering trades at ₹2,455.90. That values the enterprise at a market capitalization of ₹15,874.19 Cr (Screener: ₹15,861 Cr) [1][21]. Against TTM consolidated net profit of ₹138 Cr (TTM EPS ₹21.23) and book value of ₹247 per share, the stock commands a trailing P/E of 116x and 9.94x Price-to-Book [1]. Adding ₹578 Cr of September 2026 borrowings puts gross enterprise value above ₹16,450 Cr. That equals roughly 63x TTM EBITDA (₹260 Cr) and 24x TTM Sales (₹684 Cr) before netting treasury cash [1].

Why does the market pay 116x trailing earnings for a business generating 11.9% ROCE and 9.09% ROE [1]? Three narratives anchor that multiple. First, Azad holds a ~₹6,500 Cr rolling order book (~9.5x TTM sales) across GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and Rolls-Royce [3][10][11][12]. Second, six newly commissioned dedicated OEM facilities (44,800 sq. m.) at Tuniki Bollaram remove near-term capacity bottlenecks [16][17]. Third, investors prize its scarcity value as one of India's few NADCAP/AS9100-certified airfoil suppliers as global turbine supply chains diversify out of Western shops [4][10].

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF: What Today's ₹15,874 Cr Market Cap Already Assumes

web_blocks.html: Rather than guessing a target multiple in isolation, a Reverse DCF asks what operating reality Azad must deliver over FY27E–FY31E to earn a 12% cost of equity from ₹2,455.90 [1]. Suppose Azad compounds consolidated revenue at 30% CAGR from ₹603 Cr in FY26 to ₹2,239 Cr in FY31E and sustains a 36% EBITDA margin (₹806 Cr EBITDA). Crucially, assume it also fixes working capital so Free Cash Flow converts at 16% of revenue (₹358 Cr FCF by FY31E). Discounting cumulative FY27E–FY31E FCF plus a 28x terminal FCF multiple back at 12% yields an intrinsic value of ₹11,200–₹13,400 Cr (₹1,730–₹2,070 per share).

web_blocks.caption: AZAD Reverse DCF Sensitivity Matrix (12% WACC, 5-Year Horizon FY26–FY31E)
web_blocks.takeaway: At ₹2,455.90, investors are already paying for ~33% five-year revenue CAGR AND a full pivot from -₹691 Cr FY26 FCF to +18% FCF margins by FY31E—leaving zero room for a working-capital slip or OEM schedule delay. (Note: This 5-year FCF-discounted Base value of ₹1,960 sits below Chapter 9's 12–18 month Base Target of ₹2,340 because the latter applies a 72x multiple to FY28E EPS before full FCF normalization.)

The automated table above pulls TradingView's trailing feed. In contrast, our Screener.in consolidated ledger [1][22]–[26] shows AZAD at 38.0% TTM OPM / 116x P/E / 11.9% ROCE. Peer Screener.in figures stand at 307x P/E (8.59% ROCE) for PTCIL, 118x (10.2%) for DYNAMATECH, 137x (15.1%) for MTARTECH, 85.4x (12.6%) for BHARATFORG, and 98.3x (21.9%) for DATAPATTNS.

web_blocks.title: The Multiple Compression Trap When Cash Conversion Lags
paragraphs: MTAR Technologies [19][24] offers a live domestic cautionary tale: when working capital expands faster than revenue and customer concentration delays deliveries, a 100x+ precision-engineering multiple compresses rapidly toward 50x–70x even while the long-term technology story remains intact. AZAD's 116x P/E assumes it will avoid that exact air-pocket.

web_blocks.html: Historical Multiple & Earnings-Yield Reality Check: At ₹2,455.90 against TTM EPS of ₹21.23, AZAD's trailing earnings yield is just 0.86% [1][21]. That sits nearly 600 basis points below the Indian 10-year sovereign yield. Even if consolidated PAT doubles over two years from ₹138 Cr (TTM) to ~₹275 Cr by FY28E, the stock at today's price would still trade at ~58x forward earnings. To earn a 15% annualized return over three years, AZAD must hit ~₹350+ Cr PAT by FY29E, turn strongly FCF-positive, and keep a 70x+ exit multiple [1][16]. That leaves almost no margin of safety if global gas-turbine capex slows or depreciation outpaces revenue.

Valuation Re-Rating Trigger: We would reconsider AZAD's valuation only if audited H2 FY27 cash flows turn positive (CFO > 50% of EBITDA) alongside a price reset below ₹2,000–₹2,100 (or forward P/E compressing below 55x–60x on verified earnings).

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have completed our price-blind forensic audit of Azad Engineering—and locked in our CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL business quality verdict before ever glancing at a ticker quote—we can finally open the market ledger. As of the November 13, 2026 close, Azad trades at ₹2,455.90 per share, giving it a market capitalization of ₹15,874 crore. On trailing twelve-month earnings of ₹138 crore, that is a P/E ratio of 116 times, nearly 10 times book value, and more than 60 times trailing EBITDA.

Pause for a moment and ask yourself a simple question: what kind of business deserves 116 times earnings? Usually, only two archetypes clear that bar without breaking investors' hearts. The first is a capital-light software or platform monopoly with 80% gross margins and 100% free-cash-flow conversion. Azad is the opposite—it is a heavy-machining, alloy-forging industrial manufacturer that just burned ₹691 crore of free cash flow in FY26. The second archetype is an early-stage industrial franchise standing on the threshold of an explosive, multi-year earnings inflection where today's depressed return on capital is merely a temporary artifact of unutilized newly built factories.

That second narrative is precisely what the market is underwriting at ₹2,455.90. With six dedicated OEM facilities now commissioned at Tuniki Bollaram and a rolling order book near ₹6,500 crore, bulls argue that trailing earnings and 11.9% ROCE are backward-looking—a snapshot of a company that just finished laying down the tracks before the trains run at full speed. There is real truth in that argument. You cannot build 44,800 square meters of NADCAP-qualified capacity for GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries without front-loading capex and inventory.

Yet our job across this desk is not to repeat the bull story; it is to invert the math. When we run a Reverse DCF on ₹15,874 crore at a 12% cost of equity, we discover that today's share price already assumes Azad will compound revenue at roughly 33% every single year through FY31—reaching ₹2,500 crore in annual sales—while holding EBITDA margins above 36% and simultaneously transforming its -114% FY26 free-cash-flow margin into a positive +18% free-cash-flow margin. That is not a conservative base case; that is priced-for-perfection execution.

Compare Azad side by side with its listed Indian aerospace and precision-engineering peers. Yes, PTC Industries trades at an eye-watering 307 times earnings as it builds titanium and superalloy casting capacity, and MTAR Technologies trades at 137 times earnings. Dynamatic Technologies sits at 118 times, virtually identical to Azad's 116 times. But look one row over at Data Patterns: it generates a 21.9% ROCE and 15.9% ROE with clean defense-electronics cash conversion, yet trades at 98.3 times earnings—a lower multiple than Azad despite nearly double the return on capital. Even Bharat Forge, a global forging giant with diversified automotive and defense lines, trades at 85.4 times with a higher 12.6% ROCE.

Why does this peer spread matter to you and me? Because it exposes where the margin of safety sits. At 116 times trailing earnings, Azad is not being priced like a capital-intensive, working-capital-stretched manufacturer whose CFO was -₹119 crore last year. It is being priced as if working-capital compression to 150 days and ROCE expansion above 20% are already guaranteed. If H2 FY27 delivers that cash-conversion turn, the stock can grow into its multiple. If debtor days stay stuck near 189 days or a major turbine OEM pushes out delivery schedules by two quarters, a de-rating from 116x toward 65x–75x P/E would wipe out 35% to 45% of equity value even while revenue continues growing.

Think about the arithmetic of forward returns from ₹2,455.90. At 116 times trailing earnings, Azad's trailing earnings yield is less than 0.9%. Suppose Azad executes brilliantly and more than doubles net profit over the next two years—from ₹138 crore TTM to ₹275 crore in FY28. Even in that optimistic scenario, at today's share price you would still be paying 58 times FY28 earnings. If the market decides that a capital-intensive forging and machining business with 12% to 15% ROCE deserves 60 times forward earnings rather than 116 times, your two-year stock return is flat—all the operational heavy lifting goes merely toward growing into today's multiple. That is the classic valuation trap in high-multiple industrial growth stories.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Never Confuse a Great Factory With a Cheap Stock
book_callouts.text: You can walk through Tuniki Bollaram, admire the five-axis milling cells and the GE Vernova plaques on the wall, and rightly conclude that Azad has built something rare in Indian manufacturing. The mistake investors make is stopping there. A rare factory bought at 116 times earnings with -₹691 crore of trailing free cash flow leaves zero cushion for timing delays. Valuation is the bridge between engineering admiration and investment return.

book_subsections.title: Why Scarcity Multiples De-Rate When Capital Intensity Bites
paragraphs: In bull markets, investors often defend 100x-plus P/E ratios on Indian aerospace and defence suppliers by pointing to scarcity: there are only a handful of listed companies qualified by GE, Rolls-Royce, or Safran. Yet scarcity multiples only hold while return on incremental capital is rising and cash conversion is clean. The moment depreciation, interest expense, and working-capital debt begin growing faster than net profit—as we just saw in Azad's Q2 FY27 sequential PAT dip from ₹35 crore to ₹31 crore—institutional buyers quietly step back.

That is why our Reverse DCF exercise is so revealing. At ₹2,455.90, you are not buying Azad at a discount to its ₹6,500 crore order book; you are paying upfront for 33% annual revenue growth through FY31 AND a full pivot to +18% free-cash-flow margins. Any stumble along that five-year tightrope leaves the stock vulnerable to multiple compression toward 65x–75x forward earnings.

Look at how differently the peer table frames this risk. Data Patterns earns a 21.9% ROCE and 15.9% ROE with clean defense-electronics cash conversion, yet trades at 98.3x P/E—a full 18 turns cheaper than Azad's 116x P/E despite nearly double the return on capital. Bharat Forge trades at 85.4x P/E with a 12.6% ROCE and global scale. Meanwhile, PTC Industries at 307x and MTAR Technologies at 137x show how quickly high-multiple Indian precision names can punish buyers when working capital stretches. Paying 116x for Azad before its cash-flow turn is simply paying Bull-case pricing for a Conditional-case balance sheet.
